The study was conducted to predict the flow field within the NASA Lewis Transonic Turbine Blade Cascade Facility, which is used to evaluate rocket propulsion turbines.
A pitchwise non-uniform total pressure distribution was observed at the blade row leading edge plane.
The PARC code, a general-purpose, three-dimensional, Navier-Stokes code with multi-block solution capability, was used for the computational analysis.
The computational analysis showed that the cause of the flow non-uniformity was a pair of vortices that originated in the embedded bellmouth inlet.
An examination of the results showed that the distortions were caused by the interaction of the flow with the embedded bellmouth.
Computations were performed for an inlet geometry that eliminated the embedded bellmouth by bridging the region between it and the upstream wall.
The analysis of the redesigned inlet section indicated that eliminating the embedded bellmouth eliminated the troublesome pair of vortices, resulting in a flow with much greater pitchwise uniformity.

The computational approach was chosen because physical accessibility to the inlet section was limited, and it allowed for cheaper and quicker examination of design changes compared to an experimental approach.
The computational analysis was able to accurately predict the total pressure loss regions consistent in strength and location to experimental measurements.
The study demonstrates the usefulness of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) in analyzing and redesigning complex flow geometries in turbine cascade facilities.
